items.title: 20.1.1 Thermodynamic Stability of Benzene and Resonance

source_refs.note: Topic 20.1.1 with the first Figure 20.1 (PDF 60-61), redrawn. The book gives both '158.5 kJ/mol lower than expected' and '152 kJ/mol lower'; 360 - 208 = 152 is used. The definition of resonance is added for the learning outcome.

blocks.text: Like alkenes, benzene has double bonds in Kekule's structure, but it is much more stable than alkenes. The evidence comes from heats of hydrogenation: the heat given out when hydrogen is added over a catalyst, giving cyclohexane in each case. Cyclohexane is the common low-energy reference point.

items: So 1,3-cyclohexadiene (two C=C) would be expected to release 240 kJ/mol, and the hypothetical 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene (Kekule's structure, three C=C) 360 kJ/mol.
Benzene actually releases only 208 kJ/mol, 152 kJ/mol less than expected.

blocks.alt: An energy diagram with cyclohexane at the bottom. Arrows down to it show the heats of hydrogenation: hypothetical cyclohexatriene 360 kJ/mol, 1,3-cyclohexadiene 240 kJ/mol, benzene (actual) 208 kJ/mol and cyclohexene 120 kJ/mol. A purple double arrow marks the 152 kJ/mol gap between the expected and actual values for benzene, the resonance energy.
blocks.caption: Heats of hydrogenation of cyclohexene, cyclohexadiene, cyclohexatriene and benzene (original diagram after Figure 20.1).
blocks.long_description: The further a compound is above cyclohexane, the more energy it has and the more heat its hydrogenation releases. If benzene were cyclohexatriene it would release 360 kJ/mol; it releases only 208 kJ/mol, so it lies 152 kJ/mol lower in energy than that structure. This extra stability is the resonance (delocalisation) energy.

blocks.title: Resonance and resonance energy
blocks.text: Benzene's real structure is not either Kekule structure but a single delocalised structure between them; this is called resonance. Its pi electrons are spread over all six carbons. Resonance (delocalisation) energy is the extra stability this gives compared with the hypothetical structure with localised double bonds: 152 kJ/mol for benzene.
